planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated offsets in spring in shallow, extremely gritty mineral soil, since wild collection has devastated populations across its range.

directions: Peyote forms a flattened, spineless, blue-green to gray-green button divided into low, rounded ribs topped with tufts of woolly white hair instead of true spines. It grows extremely slowly from a large taproot, native to limestone scrub of the Chihuahuan Desert in Texas and north-central Mexico, and stays only a few inches wide even after decades in cultivation. Small pink to white daytime flowers emerge from the woolly crown in spring, followed by tiny club-shaped pink fruit. Because wild-collected material is both legally sensitive and ecologically damaging to harvest, only nursery-grown, seed-propagated stock should be planted, in a shallow pot of mineral grit with minimal summer water and none in winter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot in spring in pure mineral, gypsum-rich grit that mimics its native cliff habitat, since ordinary cactus mix retains too much moisture for this species.

directions: A monotypic genus described only in 1992, Geohintonia mexicana forms a solitary, gray-green globose stem coated in a pale bluish bloom, with 18 to 20 sharply defined ribs that give it a strongly pleated, star-like profile distinct from any related genus. Short, flattened, corky spines emerge from woolly areoles and soon dry to a brittle, papery texture that flakes away with age, leaving the ribs largely bare. Rich pink to magenta funnel-shaped flowers open at the woolly crown in spring. In the wild it grows only on near-vertical gypsum cliffs in a tiny pocket of Nuevo Leon, Mexico, so cultivated plants demand exceptionally sharp mineral drainage, full sun, and restrained watering to avoid rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in spring in gravelly, alkaline soil on a slope or raised bed so winter moisture drains away quickly from the shallow root system.

directions: This small, solitary, egg-shaped to cylindrical cactus is covered so densely in interlacing white to gray radial spines that the green stem beneath is almost entirely hidden, giving the plant an overall pale, woven appearance that separates it from spinier, darker-spined Echinomastus relatives. A single stouter central spine points downward from each areole, and small white to pale pink funnel-shaped flowers open near the crown in early spring, among the first cactus blooms of the season in its range. It grows scattered among desert grasses on gravelly limestone soils of southeastern Arizona and west Texas into northern Mexico, typically between 3,000 and 7,000 feet elevation, and needs sharp drainage, full sun, and minimal water outside of spring growth to thrive in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant in spring on a rocky, sun-baked slope or raised gravel bed to match the sharp drainage of its native grassland habitat.

directions: A cylindrical, solitary cactus of southeastern Arizona grassland and scrub, this species is named for its straight, stiffly upright central spine, usually a striking maroon-purple, that stands apart from the dense network of 12 to 18 shorter radial spines pressed close to each of the 18 to 21 narrow ribs. The overall spine coverage is thinner than in E. intertextus, leaving more of the green stem visible between areoles. Pale pink to lavender flowers cluster in a tight ring at the crown in spring, followed by small green fruit that dries brown at maturity. It requires gritty, fast-draining mineral soil, full sun, and careful winter drought to prevent the shallow roots from rotting.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a shallow, gravel-topped trough or raised bed so the tiny crown stays bone dry and well ventilated through winter.

directions: One of the smallest cacti in North America, this species forms a single spherical stem barely an inch tall, ringed by twisted, corky white to pale gray spines arranged in a soft twisted cross pattern with no true central spine, unlike the stiffer spines of most Pediocactus relatives. During drought the stem contracts and pulls nearly flush with the soil surface, making it almost invisible until pale yellow to yellow-green flowers with faint purplish midstripes open at the crown in early spring. Endemic to a narrow band of clay and shale badlands near the Little Colorado River in Arizona, it is federally protected and extremely slow-growing, so plants should only come from nursery-propagated seed. It demands gritty, alkaline mineral soil, full sun, and near-total winter dryness.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a well-draining mineral cactus mix and give a full watering-and-dry-down cycle through the growing season.

directions: Native to the mountain grasslands of Cordoba and San Luis provinces in northern Argentina, this solitary, globose cactus has 17 to 20 sharply defined ribs bristling with 6 to 10 fine radial spines and up to 4 stouter central spines. Its chief attraction is a disproportionately large flower, over an inch and a half across, in soft pastel pink or white, opening from woolly buds near the crown in summer. It is easier to bring into bloom than many South American globular cacti, but it resents hard freezes and heavy winter moisture, so it needs a fast-draining mineral mix, bright full sun, and a near-dry winter rest to perform well.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil and resume regular watering only once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: This Argentine cactus starts globular and gradually elongates into a short cylinder, usually solitary but occasionally offsetting at the base with age, and carries dense areoles of 10 to 20 yellowish-brown spines with darker tips that fade to gray as the plant matures. Its species name refers to the bristly scales covering the flower tube rather than the petals themselves, which open wide and funnel-shaped in summer in shades from white to pinkish lilac, often with a mauve outer band that deepens at higher, cooler elevations. It shares its Cordoba highland origin with Acanthocalycium klimpelianum but grows taller and more cylindrical over time. Give it full sun, sharp mineral drainage, and a dry, cool winter rest to encourage its showy summer flowers.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a gravel-mulched raised bed or scree that drains instantly, since it grows naturally hidden among high-plains grasses.

directions: Also long known as Toumeya papyracantha, this diminutive high-plains cactus is instantly recognizable for its flattened, papery, ribbon-like central spines that twist and curl as they age, so densely covering the small cylindrical stem that it resembles a wisp of dried grass more than a cactus. That camouflage is deliberate: it grows scattered among grama grass on the gravelly, alkaline plains and pinyon-juniper flats of Arizona, New Mexico, and west Texas at elevations up to 7,000 feet, where winters bring hard freezes. Small, pale flowers with dark midstripes open near the crown in spring, followed by a dry, tan fruit. Give it gritty mineral soil, full sun, and strict winter drought, since it is one of the more cold-hardy cactus species in cultivation.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
